profiles.meeting_scenario: After the spring administration of a stepwise radiology skill assessment in a medical student elective, the research team noticed that the thoracic imaging cases produced an unexpectedly high share of 'undefined' codes and noticeably lower inter-rater agreement than earlier cohorts. A radiology faculty lead and an assessment analyst meet to troubleshoot whether the problem comes from the learners, the case set, the coding rubric, or the scoring workflow before the next cohort starts in three weeks. The agenda is to review where the disagreement seems to cluster, identify the likely root cause, and agree on a practical fix that can be implemented quickly without disrupting the scheduled teaching block. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for improving reliability on the chest cases and a small verification step before the next run.

members.name: Dr. Sofia van Leeuwen
members.role: Radiology faculty lead and principal investigator for the visual diagnosis assessment study
members.expertise: Thoracic imaging, clinical reasoning in radiology, and case-based medical education
members.background: She is a consultant radiologist who designed most of the stepwise cases for the elective and has led faculty calibration sessions on coding perception, analysis, and diagnosis errors.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the educational value of the existing stepwise format and avoid reopening the student-facing test so close to the next elective; she is especially concerned that faculty time for recoding and case revision is limited.
hidden_assumptions: If a student marks the correct area but describes it incompletely or with the wrong imaging features, that is primarily an analysis error; diagnosis errors start only after the image has been adequately interpreted.
When people mention 'the chest set,' they mean the faculty-approved calibration version of the thoracic cases that she reviewed during the post-course debrief.
A 'rubric cleanup' refers to clarifying coder instructions and examples, not revising the wording of the student-facing prompts or the case package itself.
If they agree to double-code '20 cases,' that means 20 individual erroneous student-case responses sampled from the problematic subset, because that is the unit she uses in coding meetings.

members.name: Elias de Groot
members.role: Assessment analyst and psychometrician for the medical education unit
members.expertise: Scoring workflows, coding reliability, LMS-based assessment delivery, and quality control for performance data
members.background: He manages the exported response files, prepares coder packets, and monitors reliability statistics across cohorts for several clinical skills assessments.
members.private_state: He wants a defensible and reproducible coding process before the next cohort and suspects that ambiguity in the operational materials, not just coder inconsistency, is driving the thoracic-case problem.
hidden_assumptions: Once a student has localized the image finding, the difficult step of converting observed features into the right disease interpretation still belongs to analysis; diagnosis errors are relatively narrow and mostly naming slips after a coherent interpretation is already evident.
When people refer to 'the chest set,' they mean the live LMS-delivered thoracic package used by students this spring, including the substituted portable-film case and the current answer-key export.
A 'rubric cleanup' naturally includes the entire scoring package that affects coding consistency, including prompt wording, answer-key notes, and coder decision rules.

If they agree to double-code '20 cases,' that means 20 complete student tests from the spring cohort, because reliability estimates should reflect the operational scoring workflow rather than isolated responses.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an analysis error
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the chest-case disagreements are 'mostly analysis errors.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'analysis error' for mistakes in interpreting or describing the visual finding after it has been seen, while reserving 'diagnosis error' for cases where the image interpretation is adequate but the final disease label is wrong.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'analysis error' more broadly to include failures in translating observed features into the correct disease interpretation, so many cases M1 would call diagnosis errors still feel like analysis problems to him.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both rely on the same three-stage framework and use familiar coding labels from the project, so the phrase sounds fully aligned; the difference only affects edge cases, which makes the divergence hard to notice in a brief troubleshooting discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: Which thoracic case set they are talking about
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the chest set' or 'the thoracic cases' when citing where the problem sits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the faculty calibration set she last reviewed, which contains the original curated thoracic cases and faculty comments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the operational LMS package used in the spring run, which includes a substituted portable chest film and the exported answer-key mapping attached to the live scoring files.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two versions share nearly all case titles and are routinely referred to with the same shorthand, so aggregate discussion about disagreement rates sounds compatible even though one swapped case and its associated materials differ.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'cleaning up the rubric'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that they should 'clean up the rubric before the next run.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means tightening coder guidance for borderline perception/analysis/diagnosis distinctions while leaving the student-facing prompts and case wording untouched.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means revising the whole scoring package that influences coder consistency, including prompt phrasing, answer-key notes, and coder rules for the thoracic cases.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In assessment work, 'rubric' is often used loosely to cover anything around scoring, so both can sincerely agree to the same phrase while imagining different boundaries for the fix.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'double-code 20 cases next week' to check whether the fix works.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means selecting 20 individual erroneous responses from the chest subset for quick faculty recoding.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means recoding 20 full student test forms so the reliability check reflects the actual operational workflow and case mix.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The number and purpose sound shared, and both routinely use the word 'case' for the unit they personally handle, so neither feels a need to clarify the sampling frame.

turns.inner_thought: The post-course debrief on the faculty-approved calibration version of the thoracic cases did not look this unstable, so I need to understand why the chest set is suddenly being framed as the weak point. If this is mostly a coder-boundary issue, we can fix it without touching the student-facing stepwise cases. I really do not want to reopen the case package three weeks before the next elective.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What stood out to me from the spring review was how many more undefined codes we saw than expected in the chest set, and that seems to be where agreement really dropped. I want to get clear on what is actually driving that before we change anything.

turns.inner_thought: In the live LMS-delivered thoracic package, especially with the current exported key, most of the drift is clearly sitting there. And a lot of those disputed responses are analysis errors in the broad sense: students may point to the right place, but they still are not converting what they see into the right interpretation. I need Sofia to see this may be more about the operational materials than faculty coder inconsistency alone.
turns.utterance: Yes, that matches the scoring report. The thoracic cases account for most of the coder drift in the live run, and when I looked through the disputed responses, a lot of them felt like analysis errors rather than simple misses.

turns.inner_thought: I don't quite see those as analysis errors if the student has already localized the finding and given a serviceable read on it. In my framework, once the image has been interpreted adequately, the remaining mistake is a diagnosis error. That distinction matters for coder consistency, but I can keep this at the level of shared labels for now.
turns.utterance: Some of those may be getting grouped a bit too early, though. Once the student has marked the right region, several of the contested responses looked more like diagnosis errors to me, because the description step was already reasonably serviceable.

turns.inner_thought: We are probably using the same framework, but in the spring thoracic package I reviewed, many students only got as far as a plausible location. They still failed at the harder interpretive step, which I would absolutely keep under analysis. Since we're both using the same labels, I assume she mostly means the same thing and is just emphasizing a few edge cases.
turns.utterance: I see what you mean, but in the thoracic cases I reviewed, the pattern was often that they could point to a plausible area and then didn’t really turn the visual features into the right condition. That’s why I keep landing on analysis for quite a few of them.

turns.inner_thought: From the faculty calibration version, the chest set itself looked straightforward enough. The fastest path is to tighten coder guidance around perception-analysis-diagnosis boundaries, especially for partial descriptions and latent errors. We should not start altering the student prompts or case wording now.
turns.utterance: That may be, but the chest set looked fairly straightforward in faculty calibration. My instinct is that before we change too much, we should clean up the rubric for those boundary cases and see whether that resolves most of the disagreement.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on cleaning up the rubric. To me that definitely includes the operational wording and notes around the live thoracic package, especially the portable-film item and the description-step phrasing if those are feeding coder uncertainty. If we don't tighten the full scoring package, we'll just reproduce the same ambiguity.
turns.utterance: I agree, cleaning up the rubric before the next run makes sense. I’d also want to look closely at the portable-film item and the wording around the description step, in case those are contributing to the uncertainty we’re seeing.

turns.inner_thought: I need to hold the line here: no changes to what students see. We can add clearer coder examples in the thoracic materials, especially for partial knowledge and those borderline latent-error patterns, but the stepwise format should stay intact for the upcoming elective.
turns.utterance: For the upcoming elective, I’d prefer to keep the student-facing format as it is and focus on sharper coder examples instead, especially around latent errors and partial knowledge in the thoracic pack.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable if the scoring materials are part of the cleanup. I also need a defensible check that reflects the actual workflow, so double-coding 20 complete student tests from the spring cohort would let us see whether agreement improves under operational conditions. She'll likely be on board with the number and timing.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. Then let’s verify the cleanup by double-coding 20 cases next week, so we can see whether the chest-case agreement rebounds before release.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. I can quickly pull 20 individual erroneous responses from the chest subset—specifically the ones that were marked undefined or split between analysis and diagnosis. That gives us the most efficient stress test of the coder guidance without committing faculty to recoding whole scripts.
turns.utterance: Yes, let’s do that. I can pull 20 of the chest responses that were previously marked undefined or split between analysis and diagnosis, and we can use those for a quick faculty recode.

turns.inner_thought: Great, I'll prepare the sample from the spring cohort in the operational files and revise the scoring package around the thoracic problem area. I assume when she says she'll pull the cases, she means she'll identify the relevant students and I can build the 20 full test forms from there. This should give us a proper workflow-level reliability check.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll prepare the sample from the spring cohort and update the scoring materials, so we can test the revised rubric on the same thoracic problem area and see where the agreement lands.
